newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin's suave front-man rising in Kremlin.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's suave front-man rising in Kremlin.

text.p: Sergei Yastrzhembsky, the Kremlin's suave and smooth-talking front-man, is quietly but rapidly growing in influence behind the scenes as a younger generation comes to the fore in Russian politics.

President Boris Yeltsin put his 43-year-old press secretary in charge of coordinating foreign policy on Friday, less than two weeks after making him deputy head of the presidential administration. He also remains Yeltsin's spokesman.

Yastrzhembsky's rise is a reward for eight months in which he has brought a human touch and finesse to the job of getting the Kremlin's message across on everything from Yeltsin's heart problems to infighting among its leaders.

"We want to make certain efforts...to hold discussions of these subjects, in principle, in a more civilised way," Yastrzhembsky said, promising a policy of more openness after Yeltsin brought him into the Kremlin last August.

Since then, Yastrzhembsky has lifted the shutters at least some of the way on Yeltsin's health and given the Kremlin's press department a facelift, holding regular briefings which reinforce the impression of openness.

But he has also delivered tirades against NATO's plans to expand eastwards and rapped Western or Russian journalists deemed by the Kremlin to go too far in speculation about sensitive issues such as Yeltsin's health and family life.
At last month's U.S.-Russian summit in Helsinki, he ran a slick media operation which rammed home Russian concerns over U.S. policies on issues ranging from visas to global security.

Yastrzhembsky, well groomed in sharp suits, wandered a Russian media centre at the summit taking reporters' questions in Russian, French and English. After the summit, he tossed off his jacket and put on a sweater to have a beer with journalists.

Just how much influence he has is hard to gauge, although he appears to have no major say in policy-shaping. His duties until now have been largely organisational and he has done nothing to suggest he has a driving ambition for power.

Even in his new role coordinating foreign policy in the Krmelin, his main task is likely to be organisational, although he is quietly consolidating his position with his potentially influential duties in the Kremlin.

Explaining his new role, Yastrzhembsky said he would not take over directly from Dmitry Ryurikov, who was sacked as Yeltsin's main foreign policy adviser last Friday, but would coordinate his replacement's work.
"When a new presidential aide on foreign policy issues is appointed, he will cooperate directly with me," Yastrzhembsky said in a radio interview on Saturday.
He is part of a younger generation which has won its way to power since Yeltsin won a four-year second term as president last July.
They are led by first deputy prime ministers Anatoly Chubais, 41, and Boris Nemtsov, 37, whose powers far outstrip Yasztrzhembsky's.

A career diplomat, Yastrzhembsky was Russia's ambassador to Slovakia until Yeltsin promoted him last August. He had been chief Foreign Ministry spokesman for more than a year before he went to Bratislava in 1993.
The signs may be good for Yastrzhembsky if he is hoping for further success in the Kremlin. Aides say he enjoys hunting and tennis, pastimes which are also among Yeltsin's favourites.
